drug_class: Mineralocorticoid (a type of corticosteroid hormone replacement)
purpose: Fludrocortisone is used to replace a hormone that your body is not making enough of on its own. It is commonly prescribed for a condition called Addison's disease, where your adrenal glands do not produce enough natural steroids. It is also used for certain conditions that cause your body to lose too much salt through your kidneys.
how_it_works: Your adrenal glands normally make a hormone called aldosterone, which helps your body hold onto the right amount of salt and water and keeps your blood pressure stable. When your body does not make enough of this hormone, fludrocortisone steps in and does the same job. It signals your kidneys to keep sodium in your body and release potassium, which helps balance your fluids and maintain healthy blood pressure.
common_side_effects: Swelling in your hands, feet, or ankles due to fluid retention. Increased blood pressure. Headaches. Weight gain. Low potassium levels, which can cause muscle cramps or weakness. Trouble sleeping or feeling more emotional than usual.
warnings: Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor, as this can be dangerous. Tell your doctor if you notice a lot of swelling, unusual weight gain, or muscle weakness, as your dose may need adjusting. This medicine can raise your blood pressure and lower your potassium, so regular check-ups and blood tests are important. Let your doctor know if you have heart disease, kidney problems, or diabetes before taking this medication. During times of illness, surgery, or major stress, your doctor may need to adjust your dose.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose is 0.1 mg (100 micrograms) taken by mouth once a day, though your doctor may adjust this anywhere from 0.05 mg to 0.2 mg daily depending on your needs. It is best taken at the same time each day, with or without food. Your doctor will monitor your blood pressure and potassium levels regularly to make sure the dose is right for you.
